web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: What You Pay for the Toll Road: Reverse DCF, Peer Multiples & Cycle History
question: At $1,069.43 per share, what growth rate is already baked into McKesson's stock price, and how does its valuation stack up against Cencora, Cardinal Health, and Henry Schein?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; implied free cash flow growth is what you are betting on.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Desk Maxim

web_blocks.html: At the November 20, 2026 close of $1,069.43 (TradingView $1,069.72), McKesson holds a $123.51 billion market cap and a $130.95 billion standard enterprise value [24, 25]. On headline multiples, the stock trades at 27.51x trailing GAAP earnings and 20.38x forward earnings [25]. It also trades at 16.63x EV/EBITDA, 17.37x price-to-free-cash-flow (P/FCF), and a 1.33x PEG ratio [25]. Management guides FY2027E Adjusted EPS to $45.60–$46.40 ($46.00 midpoint, +17% to +19% YoY) [6, 8]. That puts the shares at roughly 23.2x current-year adjusted earnings.

To strip out multiple-expansion guesswork, we run a Reverse DCF on the $123.51 billion equity value. As Chapter 6 showed, we add $5.06 billion in opioid liabilities and $2.56 billion in redeemable noncontrolling interests to net debt [2, 3, 21]. Total enterprise claims sit near $138.57 billion. We use $5.80 billion in normalized Free Cash Flow, bridging FY2026's $5.41 billion FCF with the Wellverse spin and ~$684 million in yearly opioid payouts [2]. With an 8.5% discount rate (WACC) and 3.0% terminal growth, the market prices in 7.8% annual FCF compounding over ten years [25].

Pair 7.8% implied FCF growth with McKesson's share buybacks ($4.75 billion in FY2026), which cut the share count by 3% to 4% a year [2, 16]. The market is thus pricing in 11% to 12% long-term EPS growth. That hurdle sits below management's 12% to 16% long-term Adjusted EPS target and well below FY2027E's +17% to +19% pace [6, 8]. On a three-to-five-year basis, McKesson is not priced for perfection, even though its short-term chart is stretched.

web_blocks.takeaway: At $1,069.43, the market prices in ~7.8% FCF compounding (~11.3% EPS growth with buybacks), leaving fundamental headroom if Oncology and RxTS keep scaling.

web_blocks.html: This peer table compares McKesson's valuation multiples, return on invested capital, and leverage against its three closest U.S. distribution rivals. It shows whether McKesson's headline P/E premium reflects genuine earnings quality rather than market hype.

web_blocks.takeaway: McKesson commands the highest forward P/E (20.38x) and EV/EBITDA (16.63x) in the peer group, yet trades at the lowest PEG (1.33) and highest ROIC (76.71%) due to its superior specialty and technology profit mix [25, 26, 27].

web_blocks.html: Comparing McKesson to Cencora (COR), Cardinal Health (CAH), and Henry Schein (HSIC) shows why McKesson leads the group [25, 26, 27]. Cencora trades at 15.63x forward P/E and 12.35x EV/EBITDA on $337.40 billion in sales, but it carries 3.06x debt-to-equity and 23.63% ROIC [26]. Cardinal Health trades at 18.93x forward P/E and 15.24x EV/EBITDA with 46.57% ROIC, yet posts a thinner 1.32% operating margin and 1.53 PEG [21, 26]. Henry Schein trades at 13.91x forward P/E, but suffers from 7.22% ROIC and a Stage 4 breakdown [27]. McKesson's 1.69% operating margin, 76.71% ROIC, and 1.33 PEG justify its 1.5x to 4.5x forward P/E premium [25].

web_blocks.html: A sum-of-the-parts view shows why McKesson's 20.38x forward P/E is earned, not inflated [25]. Core U.S. drug distribution—a steady, negative-working-capital toll road—deserves 15x–16x operating earnings, matching Cencora's 15.63x [26]. By contrast, Oncology & Multispecialty (+53% FY26 segment profit, 2.96% margin) and RxTS (19.45% margin, recurring software) merit 24x–28x [2]. Blending those three units after spinning off Wellverse explains McKesson's premium over Cardinal Health and Henry Schein [9, 25, 26, 27].

web_blocks.title: Historical Valuation Cycle & FY2028E Fair Value Estimate

web_blocks.company: US Drug Wholesaler De-Rating & Re-Rating Cycle (MCK & ABC/COR)
web_blocks.mechanism: From 2015 to 2019, generic drug price deflation, PBM mergers, and opioid lawsuits hit the sector. Wall Street cut McKesson and Cencora from growth multiples down to distressed utility multiples. Once generic deflation eased, GLP-1 volume surged, and specialty oncology grew, the market re-rated those same pipes above 20x forward earnings.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: MCK forward P/E fell from ~19.5x in 2015 to ~9.5x–11.0x in 2018–2019. It then re-rated to 20.38x by November 2026 [16, 25].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Paying 20x+ forward earnings works when specialty mix and buybacks drive 14%–17% EPS growth. Multiple expansion from 20.4x will not do the work, so returns depend on earnings growth and entry price [6, 25].

web_blocks.title: 18-to-24 Month Base Case Fair Value Estimate (MCK)
web_blocks.the_number: $1,200.00 per share (18-to-24 Month Base Case Fair Value)
web_blocks.how_calculated: We anchor $1,200.00 as an 18-to-24 month compounding target on FY2029E Adjusted EPS of ~$59.10 (+12.7% YoY from FY2028E $52.44) at a flat 20.3x forward P/E—matching today's 20.38x forward P/E with zero multiple expansion (equivalent to 22.9x FY2028E Adjusted EPS of $52.44). On a strict 12-month flat-multiple check, 20.38x FY2028E EPS ($52.44) equals $1,068.73, essentially flat to CMP ($1,069.43).
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY2027E Adjusted EPS midpoint is $46.00 (+17%–19% YoY) [6]. We model 14.0% FY2028E growth to $52.44 (10.5% EBIT growth + 3.5% buybacks) and +12.7% FY2029E growth to ~$59.10, valued at a flat 20.3x forward P/E.
web_blocks.the_range: $820.00 (Bear Case: ~16.5x stressed ~$49.70 EPS) to $1,350.00 (Bull Case: ~24.5x ~$55.10 FY2028E EPS on faster PMG/Core Ventures synergies).
web_blocks.if_off: If IRA Medicare Part B rules or 340B rebate shifts cut oncology fees by 150–200 bps, or if CVS extracts steeper cuts early, fair value drops toward $820–$950.

web_blocks.html: Capital efficiency explains the rest of the valuation gap. McKesson collects from pharmacies faster than it pays drugmakers, so core distribution runs on negative working capital. That drives consolidated ROIC to 76.71%, versus 23.63% at Cencora and 46.57% at Cardinal Health [25, 26]. McKesson generates $5.41 billion to $6.00 billion in annual free cash flow on under 0.2% of revenue in capex [2, 15]. Nearly every dollar of added operating profit turns into cash for buybacks and specialty deals. That cash efficiency supports a 20.38x forward multiple as long as Oncology and RxTS grow.

Stress-testing our Reverse DCF with higher discount rates confirms the same view. Suppose we raise WACC from 8.5% to 9.0% and trim terminal growth from 3.0% to 2.5%. The market's 10-year implied FCF growth hurdle rises only to 9.2%, or ~12.7% EPS growth with 3.5% annual buybacks [2, 6]. Against FY2027E Adjusted EPS growth of +17% to +19%, the expectations bar remains realistic.

Put simply, McKesson's 20.38x forward P/E reflects confidence in its specialty shift rather than hype [25]. Entry-price discipline is the only missing piece. Waiting for $940.00–$985.00 pairs a fair multiple with a strong margin of safety.

Notice why our 12-month flat-multiple check matters so much. At today's 20.38x forward P/E on FY2028E Adjusted EPS of $52.44, 12-month fair value is $1,068.73—flat to today's $1,069.43 close [6, 25]. Chasing CMP offers zero margin of safety. Instead, our $1,200.00 Base Case is an 18-to-24 month compounding target anchored to FY2029E Adjusted EPS of ~$59.10 (+12.7% YoY from $52.44) at a flat 20.3x forward P/E (equivalent to 22.9x FY2028E EPS), which delivers 1.69:1 asymmetry from the $940.00–$985.00 pullback zone [6, 25].

book_paragraphs: Once you know a business is an elite toll road, the hardest question arrives: how much of that quality is already in the price? At the November 20, 2026 close of $1,069.43, McKesson is no longer the lawsuit-plagued bargain it was five years ago [16, 24]. The stock holds a $123.51 billion market cap and a $130.95 billion standard enterprise value [25]. You are paying 27.51x trailing GAAP earnings, 20.38x forward earnings, 16.63x EV/EBITDA, and 17.37x free cash flow [25]. Against management's fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS guidance of $45.60 to $46.40 ($46.00 midpoint), you are paying roughly 23.2x this year's adjusted profit [6, 8].

Instead of guessing whether 20.4x forward earnings feels cheap or rich, flip the telescope around and run a Reverse DCF. Remember our balance-sheet rule from Chapter 6: we do not stop at bank debt. We add $5.06 billion in opioid liabilities and $2.56 billion in redeemable minority interests, putting total enterprise claims near $138.57 billion [2, 3, 21]. We use a normalized free cash flow base of $5.80 billion, reflecting the Wellverse spin and ~$684 million in yearly opioid payouts [2]. With an 8.5% discount rate and 3.0% terminal growth, today's price assumes 7.8% annual free cash flow compounding over ten years [25].

Think about what 7.8% free cash flow growth means for an owner. McKesson spends $4 billion to $5 billion a year retiring stock, cutting the share count by 3% to 4% annually [2, 16]. Combine 7.8% cash-flow growth with 3.5% share reduction, and the market only asks for 11.3% annual EPS growth. Compare that to management's long-term goal of 12% to 16% adjusted EPS growth, and the 17% to 19% growth they are posting in fiscal 2027 [6, 8]. That tells us something vital: McKesson is not in a bubble. The earnings engine can still outrun the growth baked into the price.

Why does McKesson trade at a higher multiple than its direct rivals? Look at the peer table. Cencora trades at 15.63x forward earnings and 12.35x EV/EBITDA, while Cardinal Health trades at 18.93x forward earnings and 15.24x EV/EBITDA [26]. Henry Schein sits down at 13.91x forward earnings [27]. On the surface, McKesson looks like the priciest ticket. Yet look one column deeper: McKesson posts a 76.71% ROIC—over triple Cencora's 23.63%—and a sector-high 1.69% operating margin [25, 26]. Better yet, its PEG ratio is 1.33, the lowest in the peer group versus 1.48 at Cencora, 1.53 at Cardinal Health, and 1.42 at Henry Schein [25, 26, 27].

A sum-of-the-parts view makes that premium clear. Core U.S. drug distribution is a steady, negative-working-capital toll road that merits 15x to 16x, like Cencora [26]. On top of that pipe sit two faster, higher-margin units. Oncology & Multispecialty grew segment profit 53% in fiscal 2026 at a 2.96% margin, while RxTS earns a 19.45% margin clearing prior authorizations [2]. Once Wellverse is separated with Apollo's $1.25 billion investment, public investors own a cleaner specialty and technology compounder [9, 10].

Still, history teaches us to respect valuation cycles in drug distribution. From 2015 to 2019, generic price deflation and opioid lawsuits pushed McKesson's forward multiple from nearly 20x down to 10x [16]. Today, the multiple has swung back to 20.4x forward earnings and 16.63x EV/EBITDA, near the top quartile of its ten-year band [16, 25]. We cannot count on higher multiples to bail us out if we overpay. On a strict 12-month flat-multiple check, applying today's 20.38x forward P/E to fiscal 2028 adjusted EPS of $52.44 gives $1,068.73—essentially flat to today's $1,069.43 price. That proves why chasing at current prices offers zero margin of safety. Instead, our $1,200.00 base-case fair value is an 18-to-24 month compounding target anchored to fiscal 2029 adjusted EPS of ~$59.10 (+12.7% YoY from $52.44) at a flat 20.3x forward P/E (equivalent to 22.9x fiscal 2028 EPS), which delivers 1.69:1 asymmetry from our $940.00–$985.00 pullback zone. If IRA Part B or 340B rules squeeze specialty margins by 150 to 200 bps, fair value could reset toward $820.00.

Let's also check our bull and bear valuation bookends. In a bull scenario, Precision Medicine Group and Core Ventures synergies speed up and Wellverse separates cleanly [9, 14]. At 24.5x roughly $55.10 in FY2028 EPS, shares reach $1,350.00. In a bear scenario, policy pressure or a broad market Downtrend cuts the multiple to 16.5x stressed earnings near $49.70, or $820.00. Knowing both bookends keeps our expectations grounded before we ever look at a stock chart.

book_subsections.title: Why Negative Working Capital and 76.71% ROIC Matter for Your Multiple
paragraphs: Most investors see a 1.69% operating margin and assume McKesson is fragile and capital-hungry. In truth, the opposite holds. McKesson collects from hospitals and pharmacies faster than it pays drugmakers, so core distribution runs on negative working capital. Growth creates cash rather than using it. Add capex under 0.2% of revenue, and you get a 76.71% return on invested capital—an amazing figure for a $403 billion business [2, 25].

Compare that cash engine directly with Cencora and Cardinal Health. Cencora carries 3.06x debt-to-equity and earns 23.63% ROIC, while Cardinal Health earns 46.57% ROIC on a 1.32% operating margin [26]. Neither peer matches McKesson's scale, balance-sheet strength, and high-margin software and oncology units. When a firm turns nearly all net income into free cash flow and retires 3% to 4% of shares yearly, 20.38x forward earnings is not excessive. The catch is timing: at $1,069.43, the stock leaves little cushion if the market Downtrend compresses multiples.

That is why we anchor on $1,200.00 in our base case and $1,350.00 in our bull case, while watching the $820.00 bear floor. Buying at $1,069.43 offers just 12.2% upside to base fair value, which does not pay you for a normal 10% pullback. Waiting for the $940.00 to $985.00 shelf lifts upside to $1,200.00 to roughly 22% to 28% and widens your margin of safety. Patience turns a fair price into an asymmetric setup.

book_subsections.title: Sensitivity Check: WACC, Terminal Growth, and Opioid Cash Outflows
paragraphs: Any valuation model is only as honest as its stress tests, so let's push our Reverse DCF harder. Suppose rates stay high and we use a 9.0% discount rate instead of 8.5%, with terminal growth cut from 3.0% to 2.5%. Even under that tougher bar, the $123.51 billion market cap implies 9.2% annual free cash flow growth over ten years. Add 3.5% annual share buybacks, and the implied EPS growth bar is 12.7%. That sits right in line with management's 12% to 16% target and well below fiscal 2027's 17% to 19% pace [6, 8].

We also checked whether the $684 million yearly opioid payout distorts our free cash flow base [2]. That payout is already deducted inside operating cash flow, and the schedule ends in 2038 [2, 21]. By adding the $5.06 billion remaining liability as a debt-like claim in enterprise value while using post-settlement free cash flow, we never double-count or ignore it [2, 21]. Every way you run the math, McKesson's valuation is sound. Our discipline is purely about waiting for a better chart entry.

book_subsections.title: Buyback Math: How $4.75 Billion in Annual Repurchases Compounds Per-Share Value
paragraphs: Before leaving valuation, look at how McKesson returns cash to owners. High-dividend utilities pay out most cash as taxable income. McKesson instead pays a modest $3.40 annual dividend (0.32% yield) and puts most of its $5.41 billion free cash flow into buybacks—retiring $4.75 billion of stock in fiscal 2026 [2, 25]. Retiring $4.5 billion to $5.0 billion a year shrinks the diluted share count by 3.5% to 4.0% annually.

That buyback engine works like a quiet turbocharger for per-share value. Even if operating income grows 8% to 10%, shrinking shares by 3.5% lifts EPS by 11.5% to 13.5% before counting margin gains from Oncology or RxTS. Better yet, buybacks work even harder when shares dip into our $940.00 to $985.00 zone, since McKesson retires more shares per dollar spent.

Put Chapter 7 together, and the valuation picture is clear. McKesson is not cheap on trailing GAAP earnings at 27.51x, and it sits near the top of its ten-year EV/EBITDA band at 16.63x [25]. Yet adjust for its 76.71% ROIC, negative working capital, 1.33 PEG ratio, and +17% to +19% fiscal 2027 EPS growth, and the $123.51 billion valuation is justified [6, 25]. Our Reverse DCF proves the market only asks for 7.8% annual free cash flow growth. Instead of overpaying at $1,069.43, we target $1,200.00 base fair value and wait for a margin of safety.

To sum up the peer and cycle math: Cencora at 15.63x and Cardinal Health at 18.93x forward earnings look cheaper on P/E, yet neither matches McKesson's 1.33 PEG or 76.71% ROIC [25, 26]. When an oligopoly pairs 3.5% annual buybacks with double-digit specialty profit growth, you want to own the leader. You just want to buy it on a pullback to $940.00–$985.00 rather than after a steep run [2, 24].

Keep one final lesson from the 2015–2019 wholesaler cycle in mind. In 2018, when McKesson traded at 10x forward earnings, critics claimed generic deflation had broken wholesalers for good. Yet the physical pipes never lost value, and patient buyers who focused on cash conversion rode a re-rating back to 20.4x [16, 25]. Today, the reverse holds: the market already sees the specialty shift, so our edge comes from waiting for a pullback to $940.00–$985.00.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: At $1,069.43, McKesson is a great business at a fair-to-full multiple—not a bargain, and not a bubble. Reverse DCF asks for ~11.3% EPS growth while the business delivers 12%–19%, so patience for a dip turns fair value into asymmetric upside.
